common_name: Boone County White Corn (Historic Midwestern White Dent Corn)

planting.note: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in blocks of at least four rows; give this long-season dent corn consistent moisture through pollination.

directions: Sow in fertile, well-drained soil in blocks of at least four rows, and give this long-season dent corn a full growing season with consistent moisture through pollination for best ear fill. Boone County White originated in Indiana and Illinois in the late 1800s and became one of the most widely grown white dent corns of the pre-hybrid Corn Belt, valued for tall, productive stalks and large, well-filled ears of smooth white dent kernels. It was historically important both as a table and livestock feed corn and as breeding stock, and it still produces excellent white cornmeal and hominy for gardeners wanting to grow a piece of Midwestern agricultural history.

common_name: Krug Yellow Dent Corn (Foundation Iowa Heirloom Dent Corn)

planting.note: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; rewards a full-length warm season.

directions: Sow in blocks in rich, deeply worked soil and keep watered through tasseling and silking; this is a tall, vigorous dent corn that rewards a full-length warm season. Krug was developed by Iowa farm families in the second half of the 1800s through careful ear-to-row selection and became one of the most influential open-pollinated dent corns in American corn breeding, serving as parent stock for many of the early hybrid corn lines that transformed Corn Belt agriculture in the twentieth century. Its smooth yellow dent kernels grind into hearty cornmeal, and growing it today offers a direct link to the open-pollinated corns that underlie much of modern commercial corn genetics.

common_name: Lancaster Surecrop Corn (Pennsylvania Dutch Heirloom Dent Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns.

directions: Direct sow in blocks after soil has warmed; this variety tolerates drier conditions and lighter soils better than many dent corns, though it still performs best with even moisture during pollination. Lancaster Surecrop was developed by Pennsylvania Dutch farmers in Lancaster County and became, over generations of selection, the source of the Lancaster heterotic group that later proved foundational in commercial hybrid corn breeding across the eastern Corn Belt. Grown today, it produces sturdy stalks and well-filled ears of yellow dent kernels well suited to cornmeal and traditional livestock feed, preserving a genetic line with an outsized influence on modern corn.

common_name: Wapsie Valley Corn (Iowa Heirloom Dent-Flint Corn)

planting.note: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt.

directions: Sow in blocks of at least four rows in average garden soil; its relatively short season and dent-flint hybrid vigor make it forgiving for gardeners outside the traditional Corn Belt. Wapsie Valley is an Iowa heirloom named for the Wapsipinicon River valley and preserved by Sand Hill Preservation Farm, combining dent and flint characteristics in the same ears along with striking orange, red, and multicolor kernels. It is valued both for its ornamental appeal on the stalk and for producing flavorful cornmeal, and it has become a favorite among small-scale growers seeking a productive, easy-to-grow open-pollinated corn with real regional history.

common_name: Golden Midget Sweet Corn (Extra-Dwarf Heirloom Sweet Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers; compact stature makes it practical for small gardens and pots.

directions: Direct sow in blocks of short rows or in large containers, since its compact stature makes it one of the few sweet corns genuinely practical for small gardens, raised beds, and pots. Golden Midget was bred at a New Hampshire agricultural research station in the mid-1900s specifically to give home gardeners a fast, space-saving sweet corn, reaching only two to three feet tall while still producing petite four-inch ears of golden-yellow kernels. Its short season and small footprint have kept it a favorite heirloom for northern gardeners and anyone growing corn in limited space, and it remains a genuinely useful, if lesser-known, member of the open-pollinated sweet corn family.
